mcqs.question: Why can one OS driver support disk models from many different manufacturers without knowing their internal physical details?
options: All disk manufacturers use physically identical hardware internally
The device controller translates the device's physical complexity into a standard, CPU-friendly register interface, absorbing manufacturer-specific detail
The OS re-implements a custom driver for each physical disk model at install time
Disks don't actually have physical differences that matter to software
mcqs.explanation: The controller is the abstraction boundary — it exposes a uniform interface (registers, standard commands) regardless of what's physically happening inside the device. The OS driver only needs to speak that uniform interface, not the disk's actual physical protocol.

mcqs.question: What is the key practical difference between memory-mapped I/O and port-mapped I/O?
options: PMIO is faster in every case because it uses dedicated hardware
MMIO only works on ARM processors
Port-mapped I/O eliminates the need for device registers entirely
MMIO uses ordinary load/store instructions on addresses shared with regular memory; PMIO requires dedicated instructions and a separate address space
mcqs.explanation: MMIO maps device registers into the normal memory address space, so ordinary CPU instructions work; PMIO uses a separate I/O address space requiring special instructions like x86's in/out. MMIO isn't ARM-exclusive (ARM just lacks PMIO entirely), and neither model removes registers.

mcqs.question: Why do status registers typically use individual bits for distinct conditions (busy, ready, error) rather than one numeric status code?
options: Bit flags are required by all CPU architectures
It reduces the register's physical size to zero bits
Individual bits let software test exactly one condition with a single bitwise AND, without needing to parse or compare a full numeric value
Numeric status codes cannot represent more than one state
mcqs.explanation: Bit-per-condition layout lets driver code check one specific condition cheaply and independently of others (a device can be simultaneously busy and have a pending error, for instance). It's a design convenience, not an architectural requirement, and numeric codes could represent multiple states too — just less conveniently for independent flags.

mcqs.question: With memory-mapped I/O, what actually makes an access to a device register different from an access to ordinary RAM, at the instruction level?
options: The instruction used — device access always requires a special hardware instruction
Nothing at the instruction level — the same load/store instruction is used; the difference is entirely in which memory address is being accessed
The CPU runs in a different clock mode for device access
MMIO accesses always require a system call, even in driver code
mcqs.explanation: MMIO's defining property is that device registers are just addresses in the normal memory space — the CPU issues the identical load/store instruction it would for RAM. The specialness is entirely about which address range is being touched, not a different instruction or execution mode.

mcqs.question: Why can't a user-space application directly read a disk controller's status register?
options: Device registers are only accessible from kernel mode, so the OS can prevent two processes from issuing conflicting commands to the same controller
User-space applications lack the CPU instructions needed for any memory access
Disk controllers physically disconnect from the bus during user-space execution
It's a software convention with no actual hardware enforcement
mcqs.explanation: This is a hardware-enforced privilege boundary, not just convention — device registers live in privileged memory regions only kernel-mode code can access, precisely so the OS can serialize and control access instead of letting processes fight over shared hardware.
